title: Interview with a News Photographer
description: A radio interview with a veteran news photographer about her career, ethics, technology and advice for the next generation.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · Starting out
parts.intro: You will hear a radio presenter, Daniel, interviewing a news photographer, Hana, about how she began.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: My guest this morning has spent thirty years photographing the news, from floods to elections. Hana, welcome. Did you always want to be a photographer?

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: Not at all, Daniel. I wanted to be a doctor. I only picked up a camera because my uncle lent me his, and I took it on a school trip. When I developed the film, there was one picture of a classmate laughing, and I remember thinking, I've caught something that wasn't there a second earlier.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: And that was enough to change your plans?

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: It took a few years, honestly. I studied biology, hated the laboratory, and spent every weekend wandering around the city with the camera. Eventually a local newspaper offered me a trial week, and I stayed eleven years.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: What did a young photographer actually do on a local paper?

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: Everything nobody else wanted. Village fêtes, planning meetings, a prize-winning marrow. I used to resent it. Looking back, it was the best education I could have had, because you learn to find a picture in a dull room. Anyone can photograph a disaster. Making a committee meeting look human is the real test.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: You make it sound almost like a craft.

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: It is a craft, and I think we undervalue that. People imagine it's luck, that you simply stand in the right place. Luck matters, but it favours the person who's already there at six in the morning, waiting, and who knows which way the light will fall.

parts.title: Part 2 · Ethics in the field
parts.intro: You will hear Daniel and Hana discuss difficult decisions photographers face.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: You've worked in areas hit by terrible events. How do you decide when to lift the camera and when to put it down?

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: There's no rule, and that's what makes it hard. I ask myself two questions. Is this person aware of me, and would they mind if they could see the picture in a newspaper? If the answer to the second is yes, I generally don't take it. But the answer isn't always simple.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Can you think of a time when you got it wrong?

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: Early on, after a train accident, I photographed a man sitting on the kerb with his head in his hands. The picture was published, it was powerful, and people praised it. A week later his daughter wrote to me. She wasn't angry, just sad. She said she wished she'd been asked. I've never forgotten that.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: So what do you do differently now?

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: I talk to people, even if only for half a minute. Often they say, please, take it, I want people to know. Sometimes they say no, and I respect that. And occasionally the conversation itself changes what the picture is. I stop being an observer and start being a witness.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Some critics say that conflict photography is voyeuristic.

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: I understand why they say it, and in some cases they're right. But I'd argue the opposite risk is worse. If nobody looks, then nobody is accountable. I'd rather live with the discomfort of looking than the comfort of not knowing.

parts.title: Part 3 · A changing industry
parts.intro: You will hear Daniel and Hana talk about how technology has changed news photography.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Today, almost everyone carries a camera in their pocket. Has that made your profession obsolete?

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: That's the question I'm asked at every dinner party. And, no, I don't think so, though I'd be lying if I said nothing has changed. When something happens now, the first pictures are almost always taken by someone who simply happened to be there. They're often extraordinary, and I'm grateful for them.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: So what is left for a professional?

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: Context, mainly. A phone picture tells you that something happened. A professional's job is to tell you what it means, and to do so honestly. We check who, where and when. We refuse to alter pictures in ways that change their meaning. It's a boring answer, but trust is what we sell.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: And there are new worries, aren't there, about images generated by computers?

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: Yes, and frankly they frighten me more than any rival with a phone. If a convincing image can be produced in seconds with no camera at all, then every genuine photograph gets treated with suspicion. That's the real damage. It isn't that people will believe fakes. It's that they'll stop believing anything.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Is there a solution?

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: Partly a technical one, such as records that show where a picture came from. But mostly, I think, it's a matter of reputation. Readers have to be able to say, I trust that newspaper because it has never lied to me. That takes decades to build and one careless afternoon to lose.

parts.title: Part 4 · Advice and the future
parts.intro: You will hear the end of the interview, in which Hana gives advice to young photographers.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: We're nearly out of time, Hana. If a young person wrote to you tomorrow wanting your job, what would you say?

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: I'd say, first, don't buy expensive equipment. Everybody thinks the camera is the thing. It isn't. Spend your money on travel and your time on stories nobody else is covering. A good project about your own street is worth more than a poor copy of a famous picture.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: And the practical side? It's not a well-paid career, is it?

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: No, and I won't pretend otherwise. Most freelancers I know combine the work with teaching or other jobs, and there's no shame in that. What worries me is that young photographers are asked to work for exposure. Exposure doesn't pay the rent. Know your worth and say it politely, but say it.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Has the job taken a toll on you personally?

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: Of course. There are pictures I can't look at any more. But there's a gift in it too. I've been allowed into people's worst days and best days, and trusted. That's an enormous privilege, and it's why I still get up at six.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Last question. Is there a picture you wish you'd taken?

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: Funnily enough, yes. A woman at a bus stop, in the rain, holding an umbrella over a stranger's pram. I had the camera in my bag and didn't want to intrude. By the time I decided, the bus had come. I still think about her more than about many pictures I did take.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: A lovely place to end. Hana, thank you.
